articles.title: The expansion of kinase drug discovery: new targets, platforms and indications.
articles.abstract: In the past 25 years, kinase drug discovery has grown into one of the most thriving areas in pharmaceutical research and development. What began as a field dominated by ATP-competitive small molecules has diversified into a broad therapeutic landscape that includes allosteric and covalent inhibitors, activators, proximity-induced modulators, targeted protein degraders and antibody-based therapies, with more than 150 regulatory approvals so far worldwide. In this Review, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the current kinase therapeutic landscape, including more than 2,100 kinase-targeting agents that have entered clinical development in more than 23,000 clinical trials. We cover drug platforms, new targeting approaches, the expanding target spectrum, approvals and clinical trends. Nearly half of the canonical human protein kinases have at least one clinical-stage agent, placing kinases among the most intensively explored drug target classes. Nevertheless, development remains highly concentrated around a small set of blockbuster kinase targets, such as EGFR. We also examine the features associated with successful kinase-targeting agents and causes of agent discontinuations and regulatory withdrawal.

articles.title: Evolving Mechanisms, Enduring Goals: NICHD OPPTB Support for the Science of Therapeutics in Pregnancy and Childhood (2004-Present).
articles.abstract: The Obstetric and Pediatric Pharmacology and Therapeutics Branch (OPPTB) of the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) was formed in 2004 following the enactment of the Best Pharmaceuticals for Children Act (BPCA) of 2002, in recognition of the unique research needs of studying therapeutics in pregnant women and in children of all ages. During the past two decades, the branch has supported basic, translational, and clinical research in maternal and pediatric therapeutics, including the application of emerging technologies and training and career-development activities. Its portfolio has evolved in response to scientific, regulatory, and legislative changes and has expanded to include pediatric medical devices and a stronger focus on lactation pharmacology. This mini-review describes the evolution of these programs, selected contributions, remaining limitations, and future scientific priorities.

articles.title: Could pharmacological modulation of Cu homeostasis be a valid approach against increased reactive oxygen generation and associated oxidative stress in neurodegenerative disorders?
articles.abstract: Our society is aging. Accordingly, the incidence and prevalence of age-associated diseases are exponentially increasing. Among these diseases, neurodegenerative disorders emerge as major contributors to decreased health span. The molecular mechanisms underlying these disorders are complex and multifaceted. However, increased generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and associated oxidative stress have emerged as a potent contributor to the etiopathology of many of these disorders, including Alzheimer's Disease and Parkinson's Disease (AD and PD, respectively). In this context, changes in copper homeostasis have been described as important contributors to increased ROS generation and associated oxidative stress, and targeting Cu homeostasis has been explored as a promising pharmacological approach. In this bibliographical review, we comprehensively discuss the most relevant pharmacological approaches in the field. Most of the research articles discussed here used AD and PD models, but some studies also employed models of less common neurodegenerative disorders. The literature presented here demonstrates the promising effects of targeting Cu homeostasis to halt increased ROS generation and associated oxidative stress in neurodegenerative disorders. However, many of these studies were conducted in vitro, with only a small portion in murine models of the diseases. Consequently, further research is needed to determine whether the promising results are, in fact, translatable to human therapeutics. The urgency for these studies is real, considering the high incidence and prevalence of neurodegenerative disorders and the limited therapeutics in the field.

articles.title: Bioorthogonal chemistry-enabled multiscale engineering of cancer immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: Immunotherapy has revolutionized clinical cancer management by harnessing endogenous or engineered immune responses to eliminate tumors. However, durable and safe responses in many solid tumors remain limited by the difficulty of directing potent immunomodulation to defined tumor lesions, immune-cell interfaces, and lymphoid tissues while avoiding systemic immune-related toxicity. Bioorthogonal chemistry provides a chemical strategy to address this limitation by installing non-native reactive handles in biological systems, where they undergo selective reactions to generate covalent linkages, localized activation, or functional assembly under physiological conditions. In cancer immunotherapy, these reactions can chemically label cells and biomolecules, bridge tumor-immune interfaces, anchor or assemble therapeutic platforms within tumors, and activate immunomodulators at disease-relevant sites. In this review, we first summarize the bioorthogonal reaction principles underlying chemical tagging, covalent ligation, controlled cleavage/decaging, and in situ assembly. We then discuss how these chemistries support multiscale immune engineering, from immune-tumor interface regulation and tumor microenvironment remodeling to antigen-presenting cell programming and lymph node-targeted immune priming. Finally, we highlight current translational progress, remaining challenges, and future directions for clinical implementation of bioorthogonal strategies in cancer immunotherapy. By connecting reaction design with immune-engineering function, this Review provides a framework for understanding bioorthogonal chemistry as a site-confined and multiscale strategy for cancer immunotherapy.

articles.title: Star polymer nanomedicine: From orthogonal synthetic chemistry to precision in therapeutic interventions.
articles.abstract: Asymmetric star polymers have offered a viable platform in developing soft nanoparticles for effective therapeutic interventions in high morbidity rate diseases. Orthogonal chemistry has facilitated the construction of such branched polymeric precursors for imparting an advantageous combination of multi-tasking attributes to nanoformulations. Tailoring the overall compositions of nanocarriers is accomplished through sequential independent reactions during or post branched star polymer build-up. This has enabled dispersity which is essential in designing nanomedicine with pre-determined structure-function relationships for specific applications. It has helped expand the scope of nanomedicine through facile development of carriers for small molecule to macromolecule cargo, and their enhanced efficacy in performing multiple complimentary biological tasks. This review brings into focus the elegance of orthogonal chemistry in synthetic articulation of amphiphilic branched star polymer architectures, which is laying the foundation for precision nanomedicine to address complex biological issues. We discuss advantages of strictly controlled asymmetric branched star polymer structure in biomedical applications, and how orthogonal chemistry and star polymer composition offers opportunities in smart formulation development while expediting their bench-to-bedside translation.

articles.title: Defining the druggability of viral macrodomains in coronaviruses and alphaviruses.
articles.abstract: Viral macrodomains are ADP-ribosylhydrolases encoded within the nonstructural proteins of coronaviruses and alphaviruses-2 RNA virus families with pandemic potential. Genetic studies demonstrate that ADP-ribose binding and ADP-ribosylhydrolase activity are critical for replication in alphaviruses and select coronaviruses, such as Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus and murine hepatitis virus. In contrast, for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV) and SARS-CoV-2, this domain primarily enhances in vivo fitness by modulating the innate immune response, establishing the macrodomain as a validated antiviral target. Structure-guided and high-throughput efforts have identified selective inhibitors for SARS-CoV-2 and, more recently, early-stage inhibitors of the alphavirus chikungunya virus. Both exploit a conserved active-site architecture that organizes ligand recognition into adenine, phosphate, ribose, and oxyanion subsites. Despite screening of extensive chemical libraries, inhibitor discovery has repeatedly converged on adenine-anchored scaffolds requiring polar engagement of the oxyanion region to achieve potency. This convergence defines a structurally confined druggable corridor but reveals a persistent permeability-potency tradeoff imposed by the polarity required for catalytic engagement. Cross-family comparisons further demonstrate localized divergence that shapes selectivity and constrains straightforward scaffold portability. Here, we synthesize structural, biochemical, and antiviral advances across SARS-CoV-2 and chikungunya virus, define the current boundaries of macrodomain chemical space, and delineate the chemical and biological constraints that now govern translation of catalytic inhibition into predictable antiviral efficacy. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Viral macrodomains have emerged as compelling antiviral targets in 2 pandemic-potential virus families, coronaviruses and alphaviruses, owing to their conservation and role in virulence. This review defines the chemical space and druggability of the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and chikungunya virus macrodomains and the structural and biological constraints that must be overcome to translate catalytic inhibition into next-generation antivirals.

articles.title: A Precise Activity System for Pharmacogenetics Based on Estimation of CYP2D6 Allelic Percentage Activity from the International CEPAM Database.
articles.abstract: The polymorphic enzyme CYP2D6 contributes to the metabolism of many frequently prescribed drugs, causing substantial variability in drug exposure and treatment outcomes. Genotype-based dosing recommendations currently rely on drug-agnostic categorical CYP2D6 allele activity values (AVs), potentially leading to imprecise CYP2D6 phenotype classification and under-/overdosing of numerous medications. To further advance precision dosing, we developed a CYP2D6 percentage activity (CYP2D6-PA) framework by estimating CYP2D6 allelic percentage activity (CYP2D6-APA) from 0% (no activity) to 100% (CYP2D6*1-normalized reference activity) using tamoxifen and its active metabolite Z-endoxifen as a model substrate. By leveraging nonlinear mixed-effects modeling of the international CEPAM database (>7,000 patients from 31 studies), bias-corrected CYP2D6-APAs were estimated, considering global allele distributions, additional covariates, and limited CYP2D6 genotyping. Estimated CYP2D6-APAs spanned 0%-100%, several deviating substantially from their categorical AVs. In particular, CYP2D6*2 and *35 (normal function, AV = 1), and *17 and *29 (decreased function, AV = 0.5) showed lower CYP2D6-APAs of 64-68% and 29%, respectively. Conversely, CYP2D6*9 (decreased function, AV = 0.25) showed a higher CYP2D6-APA (52%). Each additional allele copy exhibited 68% of the activity of the first copy, less than the twofold increase assumed by AVs. Neglecting limited genotyping (alleles misclassified as reference CYP2D6*1), caused CYP2D6-APA overestimation by 1.1-fold. Using CYP2D6-APAs instead of AVs translated to changes in predicted individual Z-endoxifen concentrations (-22.3% to 40.0%). While substrate specificity of empirically derived robust tamoxifen CYP2D6-APAs requires evaluation, CYP2D6-PA provides a framework applicable to other substrates/pharmacogenes. Thus, CYP2D6-PA lays the foundation for revising genotype-to-phenotype translation systems, improving precision of pharmacogenetics-guided dosing and optimizing treatment outcomes upon prospective validation.

articles.title: First factor XIa inhibitor nabs FDA approval for stroke prevention.
Virus-inspired spiky red blood cell hitchhikers for macrophage reprogramming against lung metastasis.
articles.abstract: The development of pulmonary immunomodulators that prime anti-tumor immune responses is hindered by poor lung delivery, as current strategies show limited lung targeting beyond the liver following intravenous administration. Inspired by the natural process of virus spread to the lungs via red blood cell (RBC) carriage, we developed a biomimetic immunomodulatory platform (M-RBC) integrating silica nanoparticles with RBC-hitchhiking. Rather than relying on static encapsulation, this platform is engineered as a topography-governed, shear-responsive controlled release system. It exploits tunable surface roughness to ensure that the nanoparticles remain securely bound to RBC during normal venous circulation but rapidly dissociate upon encountering the high capillary shear stress transitions in the lungs. Among the variations tested, medium-spiked silica nanoparticles (MNPs) optimally balance macrophage activation, biocompatibility, and shear-dependent RBC detachment. Upon intravenous dosing, the M-RBC platform at an optimal nanoparticle-to-erythrocyte ratio of 150:1 exhibits the highest accumulation within pulmonary metastatic nodules and the lowest liver entrapment, remarkably alleviating the local tumor immunosuppressive microenvironment. When surface-loaded with GM-CSF or administered in combination with an anti-PD1 antibody, the platform not only significantly reduces metastatic burden but also elicits a systemic immune memory that suppresses distant tumor growth. Collectively, our findings decipher how engineering nanoscale topographies can finely govern erythrocyte hijacking and capillary shear-responsive controlled release preferentially within pulmonary metastatic niches, establishing a highly translatable paradigm to engineer next-generation site-specific immunotherapeutics.

articles.title: Advancing Clinical Trials and Precision Medicine in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy Using Machine Learning-Based Trajectory Modeling and MRI Radiomics.
articles.abstract: Given heterogeneous progression of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), accurately characterizing individual disease trajectories is critical for effective clinical trials and therapeutic development. In this study, we applied machine learning (ML) approaches leveraging disease progression models and baseline magnetic resonance (MR)-derived radiomic features to quantify individual-level DMD progression trajectories and support quantitative characterization of disease progression. Radiomic features were extracted from segmented soleus (SOL) and vastus lateralis (VL) fat-fraction maps, generating 810 features per individual, with additional functional and demographic measures incorporated as covariates following feature selection. Multiple ML regressors were trained and validated to estimate MR-spectroscopy fat-fraction trajectory descriptive parameters: DPT50 (age at half-maximal increase), DPmax (extent), γ (rate), S0 (extrapolated measure at age 0). Key radiomic features were identified through feature importance analyses, followed by downstream analyses, including unsupervised clustering. The tree-based XGBoost regression model demonstrated best future longitudinal fat-fraction trajectories (SOL: mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.04, R2 = 0.94; VL: MAE = 0.06, R2 = 0.95). Subsequent downstream analyses highlighted potential key biomarkers clinically associated with DMD progression. Clustering analysis revealed clinically meaningful slow- and fast-progression subgroups with interpretable decision criteria (SOL: DPT50 = 12.21 vs. 14.83; γ = 8.07 vs. 7.54, VL: 10.37 vs. 14.21; γ = 7.72 vs. 7.09) that can inform clinical trial designs and therapeutic effects within homogenous groups. Individual-level feature importance interpretation further shows the possibility of tailoring personalized intervention strategies. These findings highlight the potential of ML-based trajectory modeling approaches leveraging baseline MRI radiomics for advancing AI-assisted clinical trial development and precision medicine, charting a new direction for MRI-guided disease modeling in neuromuscular disorders.

articles.title: Interpretable multimodal network analysis of lipid-lowering therapies.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Multimodal integration of clinical and omics data could clarify the hepatic mechanisms of lipid-lowering therapies, but interpretable methods for heterogeneous data remain limited. The objective was to apply interpretable multimodal networks (IMNs), a topology-aware framework that condenses heterogeneous omics and clinical data into compact, cross-modal modules, to characterize treatment-specific hepatic responses to simvastatin and ezetimibe. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: In the Stockholm Study, patients scheduled for cholecystectomy were randomized for 4 weeks to simvastatin, ezetimibe, their combination or placebo. We integrated liver transcriptomics and DNA methylation with plasma/bile biochemistry, including lipoprotein functionality, on the human protein-protein interactome to build treatment-specific IMNs and evaluated selected network-derived predictions in a human hepatocyte-like model (SOAT2-only-HepG2). KEY RESULTS: IMNs reduced dimensionality while preserving network topology, producing distinct molecular signatures for simvastatin, ezetimibe and combination therapy that mapped to different biological processes; the placebo network was less multimodal and more fragmented. IMNs highlighted apolipoprotein-centred modules and predicted drug effects on APOA2, PPARA and PTPRS, linked to plasma C-peptide. In SOAT2-only-HepG2 cells, selected predictions were supported experimentally, including APOA2 induction and ezetimibe-associated PTPRS upregulation. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: IMNs provide a practical, interactome-based route from multimodal patient data to focused, testable hypotheses about lipid-lowering therapies, yielding compact features suitable for downstream predictive modelling while retaining biological interpretability.

articles.title: Comparing Machine Learning and Population Pharmacokinetic Approaches for Drug Concentration Prediction in Dense and Sparse Data Settings.
articles.abstract: Population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) models, the gold standard for drug concentration prediction, are relatively complex and time-consuming; machine learning (ML) excels with high-dimensional data but remains exploratory. This study systematically evaluated seven ML algorithms-Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit with Decay (GRUD), Phased Long Short-Term Memory (PLSTM), Neural Controlled Differential Equations (NCDE), and Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (NODE)-and their heterogeneous XGBoost-based ensembles against PopPK across three data settings: dense phase I trial data; simulated dense data: linear absorption and elimination (LL), Michaelis-Menten absorption with linear elimination (MMA), linear absorption with Michaelis-Menten elimination (MME); and sparse therapeutic drug-monitoring (TDM) data. On two dense trial data, BiLSTM showed low systematic bias (F30 = 48.44%, MdPE = -6.86%; F30 = 50.62%, MdPE = 1.08%), whereas NCDE (F30 = 50.00%, MdPE = -19.39%) and NODE (F30 = 62.96%, MdPE = 11.77%) achieved the highest F30 values, respectively, compared with PopPK (F30 = 37.50%, MdPE = 24.73%; F30 = 61.73%, MdPE = 14.88%). BiLSTM showed robust extrapolation across LL, MMA, and MME datasets (F30 ≥ 75%, |MdPE| ≤ 10%). XGBoost lacked extrapolation ability, limiting ensemble gains. On sparse single-point prior data, XGBoost (F30 = 23.61%, MdPE = -8.42%) was most robust, while PopPK failed to converge. On multi-point sparse prior data, XGBoost (F30 = 26.84%, MdPE = -5.88%) outperformed PopPK (F30 = 23.63%, MdPE = -13.88%). In single-point sparse posterior prediction, PopPK (F30 = 29.71%, MdPE = 2.32%) performed best, while several ensembles improved over their neural network components. Overall, BiLSTM showed strong performance in dense data, XGBoost performed best in the prior sparse scenarios, and PopPK retained the advantage after prior concentration information was incorporated. ML approaches achieved similar accuracy to PopPK with unique advantages, representing promising tools for drug concentration prediction.

articles.title: Antiviral Activity and Safety of Molnupiravir in Healthy Participants Inoculated With Influenza Virus: A Phase 2a, Randomized, Human Challenge Trial.
articles.abstract: Influenza viruses cause substantial global morbidity and mortality. Molnupiravir, an orally administered prodrug of β-D-N4-hydroxycytidine, has broad activity against RNA viruses, including influenza. A phase 2a, randomized, two-part human challenge trial in healthy adults (NCT05818124) was conducted to evaluate molnupiravir for influenza infection. In Part 1, 20 participants were inoculated with 106.26TCID50 of A/France/759/21 (H1N1) to establish infectivity, pathogenicity, and safety. After assessment of Part 1, a 10-fold lower virus dose was selected for Part 2 to delay time to peak viral load (PVL). In Part 2, 141 participants were randomized 1:1:1:1 to receive molnupiravir (5 days, 800 mg twice daily) postexposure prophylaxis (PEP; initiated 12 hours after inoculation), molnupiravir treatment (initiated 48 hours after inoculation), oseltamivir treatment (5 days, 75 mg twice daily, initiated 48 hours after inoculation), or placebo. Primary endpoints, assessed by quantitative viral culture, were PVL in all participants for PEP and viral load area under the curve (VL-AUC) in participants with confirmed infection for treatment. Lowering the viral inoculum delayed PVL by ~12 hours, although infection rates in the Part 2 placebo arm (40%) were lower than in Part 1 (75%). Molnupiravir PEP did not significantly reduce PVL compared with placebo but was associated with lower viral burden (difference in mean log10 VL-AUC -2.21 day*log10TCID50/mL; P = 0.03). No significant antiviral effect was observed with molnupiravir or oseltamivir treatment compared with placebo. Molnupiravir was well tolerated, with an adverse event profile similar to placebo. Although primary endpoints were not met, early administration of molnupiravir showed antiviral activity.

articles.title: Spatial iron routing in breast cancer: Context-dependent vulnerabilities and pharmacological challenges.
articles.abstract: Iron supports breast cancer growth, but responses to its perturbation depend on intracellular distribution, metabolic demand and redox defence. This Review examines the mechanistic basis of iron routing and route-directed pharmacology in breast cancer. Spatial iron routing comprises acquisition, release, transfer and chemical processing from defined sources to functional destinations, including compartmental retention. Breast cancer experiments connect endosomal iron handling to respiration, regulated ferritin mobilisation to lipid oxidation, and redox-active iron-sulfur proteins to tumour-cell fitness. We propose that vulnerability depends on the relationship between accessible iron, the functions it sustains and the capacity to adapt. Functional restriction and oxidative injury can coexist, so a respiratory deficit alone cannot predict the direction of tumour response. Evidence concentrates on triple-negative models; selected oestrogen receptor-positive and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-positive models reveal treatment-state dependencies without establishing subtype-wide routing rules. Pharmacological interpretation separates intracellular exposure, target contribution and tumour endpoints. Haem-derived supply through membrane-associated RING-CH-type finger 5 (MARCH5; RING, really interesting new gene) and haem oxygenase-2 (HO-2) at mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contacts remains an unvalidated cross-system candidate mechanism in breast cancer. Integrating routing with metabolic demand and redox defence yields testable explanations for experimental responses; added value for predicting patient benefit requires validation.

articles.title: Pharmacological modulation of FoxO1 in regulatory T Cells: A strategy to reinforce immune tolerance in autoimmune and neurodegenerative diseases.
articles.abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) contribute to immune homeostasis and can modulate neuroinflammatory responses, although their functional states differ across central nervous system (CNS) disorders. Forkhead box O1 (FoxO1) is an experimentally established regulator of Treg suppressive function, transcriptional identity, and inflammatory restraint. Genetic studies demonstrate that Treg-specific FoxO1 deficiency disrupts immune regulation and permits aberrant inflammatory gene expression, while PI3K-Akt signaling controls FoxO1 phosphorylation and nuclear localization. These findings provide a mechanistic foundation for investigating FoxO1-dependent Treg dysfunction in neuroinflammation. However, the complete sequence linking inflammatory cytokines, sustained Akt activation, FoxO1 nuclear exclusion, ex-Treg conversion, and neuronal injury has not been demonstrated as a unified causal pathway in human CNS lesions. Evidence from experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis and other preclinical models supports the therapeutic potential of antigen-directed Treg approaches, while early clinical studies of adoptive Treg therapies in autoimmune disease and transplantation establish a broader translational foundation for Treg-based immunomodulation. We therefore examine FoxO1 as a candidate therapeutic regulator whose modulation may improve Treg stability, rather than as a clinically validated CNS target. Pharmacological preservation of FoxO1 activity and genetic engineering approaches, including phosphorylation-resistant FoxO1 variants, warrant further investigation through direct functional and disease-relevant validation.

articles.title: Engineering dual-targeted lipid nanocarriers for precision delivery of quercetin in breast cancer therapy: a comprehensive review.
articles.abstract: A significantly higher mortality rate in breast cancer than in lung cancer worldwide raises serious concerns despite advances in biomarker research and diagnosis. Conventional chemotherapeutics are usually associated with poor tumor selectivity, multi-drug resistance, adverse effects due to the conventional route of administration and high doses, and systemic toxicity, which restricts the therapeutic outcome in breast cancer management. Several phytocompounds have recently been investigated for potential anticancer activity, and some bioactive molecules have also entered into clinical trials. Quercetin, a naturally derived flavonoid, has drawn significant attention due to its modulation of multiple molecular pathways involved in cell proliferation, apoptosis, angiogenesis, oxidative stress, inflammation, and metastasis in breast cancer. However, its poor pharmacokinetic properties lead to limited oral bioavailability in medical applications. Thus, this review article summarizes recent advancements in quercetin-loaded lipid-based nanotherapeutics for breast cancer targeting. This extensive manuscript summarizes the phytochemistry and derivatives of quercetin, along with the demand for lipid-based delivery approaches compared to other nanotherapeutics. Recent advances in quercetin-loaded nanosuspensions, emulsions, solid lipid nanoparticles, nanostructured lipid carriers, hybrid nanoparticles, etc., are discussed, focusing on the physicochemical, pharmacokinetic properties, and molecular targeting capabilities. Furthermore, the review highlights preclinical evidence demonstrating enhanced cytotoxicity, improved bioavailability, increased apoptosis, metastasis, and reduced systemic toxicity compared with free quercetin. A few clinical translation approaches, along with the persistent challenges, are also discussed in this article. The overall understanding of this "single-platted" article further showcases an unexplored dimension to advance the knowledge of quercetin-based lipid nanoformulations for breast cancer therapy.

articles.title: Inhalable nanodelivery strategies for overcoming the pathological cascade of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
articles.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive and ultimately fatal interstitial lung disease characterized by persistent epithelial injury, immune dysregulation, fibroblast activation, excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition, and irreversible architectural remodeling of the lung. Although currently approved antifibrotic therapies can slow disease progression, their inability to reverse established fibrosis, together with systemic toxicity and limited drug accessibility to fibrotic lesions, continues to restrict therapeutic efficacy. Inhalation-based drug delivery has emerged as a promising approach for improving local drug exposure while minimizing systemic adverse effects. In particular, inhalable nanodelivery systems provide versatile platforms for enhancing pulmonary retention, improving lesion accessibility, and overcoming the biological barriers associated with fibrotic lungs. In this review, the major pathological mechanisms underlying IPF are briefly introduced to provide the biological context for therapeutic intervention. Emphasis is placed on the biological barriers that limit pulmonary drug delivery, including airway mucus, alveolar macrophage clearance, and the dense fibrotic ECM. Recent advances in inhalable nanotherapeutics designed to overcome these barriers are highlighted, including strategies for improving mucus and ECM penetration, remodeling pathological microenvironments, regulating fibrosis-associated signaling networks, and promoting tissue repair. This review adopts a pathology-oriented perspective to illustrate how the pathophysiological features of IPF can guide the rational design of inhalable nanomedicines. Finally, current translational challenges and future opportunities are discussed, providing insights into further development of inhalable therapeutics for more effective control of IPF.

articles.title: Reprogramming tumor network resilience: chemical biology, nanomedicine, and intelligent oncology for clinical translation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The dynamic interactions between the signaling networks, the intracellular organelles and the tumor microenvironment (TME) are increasingly recognized to be a systems-level phenomenon in the development of resistance to cancer. Individual molecule and pathway levels signaling, rewiring have failed to cure the clinical disease with compensatory measures. PURPOSE: This review proposes an integrated framework for understanding cancer as a network-mediated disease, shaped by intra-organelle communication and microenvironmental cues, and examines how this systems-level view can inform the design of more effective therapeutic strategies. METHOD: This review provides an integrated approach to cancer as a network mediated disease controlled by intra-organelle communication and microenvironmental signals. Therapeutic sensitivity or resistance is highlighted by key molecular relay systems as ROS-mediated signaling, unfolded protein response (UPR), calcium flux and autophagy-apoptosis. Nanomedicine as systems-level modulator that controls these networks by stimulus responsive therapeutic release, through intracellular trafficking and organelle specific targeting through controlled drug delivery. Emerging nanomedicine strategies designed to modulate resistance-associated pathways are discussed alongside evidence from preclinical studies and established nanomedicine applications, with particular attention to intracellular delivery, organelle targeting, and stimulus-responsive therapeutic release. In addition, modern computational oncology, including network pharmacology, machine learning, and multi-omics, is analyzed for the use in predictive modelling of tumor adaptation and rational design of multi-target drugs. CONCLUSION: This review provides a roadmap for taking systems-level therapeutic strategies to clinical practice by offering an overview of the advances in molecular medicine, drug delivery, and computational oncology. Hence, this review highlights the urgency of transition from reducing strategies towards adaptive strategies for tumour network resilience, and addressing MDTs.

articles.title: Metabolic-translational control of NK cell fitness under chronic stress.
articles.abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells are critical mediators of immune surveillance, yet their functional capacity is frequently compromised by chronic metabolic and environmental stress. Although metabolic reprogramming is recognized as a major determinant of NK-cell activity, how metabolic capacity is coordinated with translational control to sustain effector function and cellular persistence remains poorly understood. This review examines NK-cell fitness as a dynamic metabolic-translational balance in which nutrient availability, mitochondrial function, redox homeostasis, and nutrient-sensing pathways determine the resources available for biosynthesis, while translational control regulates their allocation toward effector protein production, adaptation, and cellular maintenance. We highlight eukaryotic elongation factor-2 kinase (eEF2K) as a mechanistically defined regulator of translational elongation with direct evidence of relevance to NK-cell function, while Nucleus Accumbens-Associated Protein 1 (NAC1) is considered a candidate regulator of NK-cell metabolic adaptation whose role remains to be established. We propose that the interaction between metabolic capacity and translational demand may determine whether NK cells maintain function or become dysfunctional under persistent stress. This framework provides a rationale for engineering NK cells with greater metabolic-translational reserve and resilience to metabolically restrictive tumor microenvironments, with potential implications for improving the persistence and therapeutic efficacy of adoptive and CAR-NK cell therapies.

articles.title: The mitochondrion as a mechanometabolic conductor of cancer metastasis: pharmacological insights from the mitochondria-peroxisome interface.
articles.abstract: Metastasis demands more than sustained ATP production: cancer cells must move organelles, remodel membranes, manage oxidative stress, and reprogram metabolism as they pass from invasion to distant colonisation. Mitochondria sit at the centre of this adaptation. This Review organises their contribution around four linked axes: deployment to the cell cortex and invadopodia; reactive oxygen species and metabolite signalling; VDAC1-dependent metabolite, calcium, apoptotic and mtDNA gating; and HIF-1α-BNIP3-dependent remodelling of the mitochondrial pool. We then ask how this mitochondrial programme is altered by peroxisomes. The two organelles share components of the fission machinery, coordinate lipid-derived substrate use and cellular redox balance, and divide tasks in hydrogen-peroxide control, ether-lipid synthesis, organelle quality control and MAVS signalling. These connections matter pharmacologically. A DRP1- or redox-directed intervention may affect both organelles, whereas VDAC1 provides a more mitochondria-restricted target logic. Peroxisomal pathways are also context dependent: fatty-acid shortening and ether-lipid synthesis can increase metabolic flexibility and membrane remodelling, yet the same pathways may raise oxidative stress or create ferroptotic susceptibility. By separating established molecular links from mechanisms that remain untested in metastatic models, we propose a hierarchical view in which mitochondria remain the principal mechanometabolic conductor, while peroxisomes set important boundary conditions for substrate use, redox signalling, immune responses and therapeutic selectivity. We also state the limitation this framing carries. The mitochondrial arm of the framework rests on direct experimental evidence, whereas a causal contribution of mitochondria-peroxisome contacts to invasion, transit or colonisation has not been demonstrated: it is inferred here from contact biology characterised without testing metastatic endpoints, from division machinery shared between the two organelles, and from biochemical coupling. The interface is therefore advanced as a testable framework for target selection and pharmacological attribution, not as an established driver of metastasis.

articles.title: Neuroprotective effects of combination of ezetimibe and sericin against lead-induced neurotoxicity.
articles.abstract: Chronic exposure to environmental pollutants, particularly heavy metals, has become a global health concern, reducing longevity. Among these, lead (Pb2+) is associated with neurobehavioral, neurodevelopmental, and neuropsychological impairments. Consequently, growing interest focuses on pharmacological and natural agents that restore neurotrophic signaling. Therefore, this study investigates neuroprotective effect of ezetimibe, an anti-hyperlipidemic agent, and sericin, a natural protein, in Pb2+-induced neurotoxicity in rats. Adult Wistar rats were divided into seven groups: control, lead acetate (PbAc2; 50 mg/kg), ezetimibe (10 and 20 mg/kg), sericin (200 and 400 mg/kg), and a combination of ezetimibe (10 mg/kg) and sericin (200 mg/kg) with PbAc2. PbAc2 was administered for 55 days, while ezetimibe and sericin treatment was initiated on days 29-55. Behavioral assessments, including grip strength, open field test, and Morris water maze test, were performed. On day 56, animals were sacrificed, and hippocampal tissues were collected for neurochemical (GABA, GAD1, and dopamine) and mitochondrial complex 3 estimation, along with hippocampal histology. The qRT-PCR (Bax, Bcl2, caspase - 3, CREB, BDNF), western blot (IGF-1R, GLP-1R, PI3K, pAkt) were performed. The results demonstrated that PbAc2 exposure induced behavioral deficits, neurotransmitter imbalance, disrupted mitochondrial-associated apoptotic pathway, and impaired neurotrophin signaling. Contrarily, ezetimibe and sericin, individually and in combination, significantly attenuated neurobehavioral impairments, restored neurochemical levels, improved mitochondrial complex III activity, suppressed apoptotic signaling, and preserved hippocampal histoarchitecture and enhanced synaptic plasticity through involvement of IGF-1R/GLP-1R signaling pathway. These findings suggest that ezetimibe and sericin, in combination, represent promising therapeutic candidates for mitigating PbAc2-induced neurotoxicity.

articles.title: Cannabis-based medicinal products for post-traumatic stress disorder: a two-year prospective analysis from the UK medical cannabis registry.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterised by persistent psychological symptoms following exposure to trauma. Cannabis-based medicinal products (CBMPs) have promising therapeutic potential. However, there is a paucity of long-term studies investigating their use. OBJECTIVES: This prospective case series aimed to assess changes in patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and the prevalence of adverse events in patients prescribed CBMPs for PTSD. METHODS: Patients enrolled on the United Kingdom Medical Cannabis Registry for PTSD were included. Changes in PROMs (Impact of Events Scale-Revised (IES-R), Generalised Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), Single-Item Sleep Quality Scale (SQS) and EuroQol 5-Dimension 5-Level questionnaire (EQ-5D-5​L)) were assessed from baseline up to 24 months. RESULTS: In total, 446 patients were included, of which 75.11% (n = 335) were already using cannabis before starting treatment. Mean IES-R, GAD-7, SQS and EQ-5D-5​L scores improved relative to baseline at all follow-up times (p < 0.001). At 24 months, 64.57% (n = 288) of IES-R data were imputed. The mean IES-R fell from 59.58 ± 15.93 at baseline to 36.91 ± 18.56 at 24 months, with 55.38% (n = 247) of patients continuing to meet the DSM-IV threshold for PTSD at 24 months. Seventy-five patients (16.82%) reported at least one adverse event. Of 578 events, 83 (14.36%) were severe, and 2 (0.35%) life-threatening or disabling. CONCLUSION: In this uncontrolled case series, CBMP treatment was associated with improvements in mean PTSD symptom, anxiety, sleep, and health-related quality of life scores. However, the improvement was concentrated within the first month and then plateaued. The observational design, high attrition, and reliance on imputed data preclude any inference of efficacy or causality.

articles.title: Pharmacokinetic determinants, clinical efficacy, and safety of teicoplanin in adults: a correlative analysis of plasma concentration and treatment outcomes.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to develop and validate a high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) method for the determination of plasma teicoplanin concentrations, identify factors influencing teicoplanin exposure in adult patients, and assess its clinical efficacy and safety. METHODS: A cohort of 125 adult patients who received teicoplanin therapy at the Second Hospital of Hebei Medical University between June 2022 and March 2023 were retrospectively enrolled. Trough plasma teicoplanin concentrations were determined using a validated HPLC method with quetiapine fumarate as the internal standard. Clinical data, including demographic characteristics, infection type, laboratory parameters, and treatment outcomes, were collected. Logistic regression analyses was conducted to evaluate the clinical efficacy of teicoplanin, attainment of target trough concentrations, and factors associated with these outcomes. RESULTS: The HPLC method demonstrated high specificity, satisfactory linearity over the concentration range of 1.5625-100 μg/mL, and acceptable precision, recovery, and stability. Under the standard dosing regimen, only 45.6% of patients achieved a teicoplanin trough concentration (Cmin) > 10 mg/L. The overall clinical efficacy rate was 87.20%, and the bacteriological clearance rate was 82.61%. Adverse events included renal injury (8.80%) and hepatic injury (1.60%), with renal injury occurring more frequently in patients with higher Cmin values. Bivariate analysis showed that teicoplanin trough concentrations were significantly associated with creatinine clearance (CrCL) and plasma albumin levels. Patients with severe renal impairment (CrCL <30 mL min-1) were more likely to achieve the target trough concentration. In addition, the incidence of renal injury increased significantly when the trough concentration exceeded 20 mg/L. CONCLUSION: A reliable, accurate, and reproducible HPLC method for the therapeutic drug monitoring of teicoplanin was successfully developed and validated. Application of the validated method presented substantial interindividual variability in teicoplanin plasma concentrations, with CrCL and plasma albumin identified as major factors associated with drug exposure. These findings provide a reliable analytical foundation for future studies of individualized teicoplanin dosing. However, given the retrospective observational design and the absence of real-time therapeutic drug monitoring-guided dose adjustment, the observed associations between trough concentrations and clinical outcomes should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than causal.
